details.claim: The Chicxulub crater is an impact crater buried underneath the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico.
The crater is estimated to be 200 kilometers in diameter and is buried to a depth of about one kilometer beneath younger sedimentary rocks.
The impact site was a marine carbonate platform, 650 meters deep at its center.
The crater is one of the largest impact structures on Earth, alongside the much older Sudbury and Vredefort impact structures.

details.extra_statement: In the late 1970s, geophysicists Glen Penfield and Antonio Camargo were mapping the Gulf of Mexico. They noticed a circular anomaly, a possible impact crater buried under the Yucatán Peninsula.
In 1991, Penfield and Alan Hildebrand confirmed it was the Chicxulub crater, linked to the K–Pg extinction.
The impact site was a marine carbonate platform, 650 meters deep at its center, with water depths varying from 100 meters on the western edge to over 1,200 meters on the northeastern edge.
Today, the crater is 300 kilometers wide, with a buried peak ring, making it one of the largest impact structures on Earth.
